passage: Jamal had been at the Leeds engineering firm for two years and still hadn't been promoted. His appraisals always said 'meets expectations', which told him nothing. One Friday he asked Lars, a senior engineer he respected, to lunch. "What would it take for me to lead a project?" he asked. Lars chewed for a while. "Honestly? You do great work but nobody sees it. You never present in meetings." Jamal's face went hot. He'd thought quiet good work was enough. Lars offered to let him present part of their next review, and said he'd mention Jamal's name when senior staff asked for someone reliable. Jamal agreed, then went home and practised in front of his mirror for an hour.

qa.q: How long had Jamal been at the Leeds firm?
qa.a: He had been there for two years.

qa.q: How did Jamal feel when Lars said nobody saw his work?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and surprised, because his face went hot and he had believed quiet good work was enough.

qa.q: What was smart about Jamal's question to Lars?
qa.a: He asked a specific, honest question about what it would take to lead a project, which got him real feedback instead of vague praise.

qa.q: How does Lars see his own role in Jamal's growth?
qa.a: He sees himself as someone who can open doors, by offering presenting chances and recommending Jamal to senior staff.

grounding: Shows a young professional seeking honest feedback and gaining a sponsor for growth.

passage: In the break room of the pharmaceutical lab, Preeti held her appraisal form. "Good" in every box. She knocked on Yusuf's cabin door, the senior scientist who'd reviewed her. "Sir, 'good' doesn't help me grow. What's one thing I should work on?" Yusuf blinked, then put down his pen. "Your reports are thorough but late. And you don't ask for help until you're stuck." It stung. She nodded and wrote it down. "What does someone ready to lead a study look like, to you?" He listed three things. She made a plan and asked if they could meet once a month to check. Yusuf agreed. Walking out, she felt oddly better. At least now she knew.

qa.q: What word appeared in every box of Preeti's appraisal?
qa.a: The word 'good' appeared in every box.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel when she heard Yusuf's criticism, and what shows it?
qa.a: It stung, but she nodded and wrote it down, showing she wanted to learn more than she wanted to defend herself.

qa.q: What small step helped Preeti turn feedback into growth?
qa.a: She asked what someone ready to lead a study looks like, then set up monthly check-ins.

qa.q: How might Yusuf see Preeti after this conversation?
qa.a: He probably sees her as serious about growing, since few juniors ask for honest criticism and a plan.

grounding: Shows a young scientist asking for specific feedback and planning her growth toward leading a study.

passage:
Dear Ujjwal sir,

Thank you for meeting me last week. I have been thinking about what you said.

You told me my code is solid but that I say yes to every task, so nobody knows what I'm actually good at. I didn't enjoy hearing that, if I'm honest. But you're right.

I'd like to aim for a tech lead role in about eighteen months. To get there, I'm going to focus on backend performance, since you said it's where the team is weakest. I'll say no to some smaller tasks and explain why.

Would you be willing to meet every two months and tell me honestly if I'm on track? I'd also be grateful if you'd suggest my name when the next performance project comes up.

Thank you for being straight with me.

Tanvir

qa.a: Tanvir didn't enjoy hearing it, but came to accept it was true.

passage: Shankar, you asked what changed in my second year at the firm. Honestly, I used to think promotion came if I kept my head down and worked late. It didn't. My appraisal said 'meets expectations', and I sulked for a week. Then I did something uncomfortable. I asked three people, my manager, a senior from another team and a peer, one question: 'What's one thing I should do differently to grow?' Two said the same thing: I never presented my own work; my manager always did. Ouch. So I volunteered to present our quarterly results. I was terrible the first time. The senior from the other team, Neha, stayed back to give me pointers, and later she mentioned my name in a leadership meeting. That's what a sponsor is, I learned. I also wrote down the next role I wanted and told my manager directly.

qa.q: What did the narrator's appraisal say?
qa.a: 'Meets expectations'.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel after the appraisal, and why?
qa.a: Disappointed and sulky for a week, having assumed hard work alone would bring a promotion.

qa.q: What steps helped the narrator plan for growth?
qa.a: Asking several people for one honest change, acting on the pattern by presenting their own work, and telling the manager the role they wanted.

qa.q: Why might Neha have mentioned the narrator's name in a leadership meeting?
qa.a: She had seen the narrator take feedback seriously and improve, so she felt confident vouching for them.

grounding: A young professional describes seeking honest feedback, gaining a sponsor and planning their next role.

passage: I've shared a pod with Tejas for two years in the hospital's IT department, so I saw this up close. When he missed out on the team-lead role last spring, he went quiet for a few days; I couldn't tell if he was angry or just thinking. Then he did something I've never done: he booked a slot with the head of department and asked, straight out, what he'd need to show to be ready next time. He came back with a list: handle vendor calls, mentor the new joiners, write clearer documentation. Over the next months I watched him take the vendor calls nobody wanted and sit with two interns every Friday. He also started having coffee once a month with Dr. Menon, who chairs the IT committee. This spring the role opened again. Tejas got it. I think he'd planned it for a year.

qa.a: Handling vendor calls, mentoring the new joiners and writing clearer documentation.

passage: Elizabeth, you're waiting for someone to notice you. I did that too, for four years. Let your Sangeeta Ma'am tell you. At twenty-five I was the best coder on my floor at a bank in Chennai. I knew it; I thought everyone knew it. Promotion lists came out twice, and my name wasn't on either. I cried in the ladies' room and said nothing. Then an older colleague, Rebecca Joseph, found me there. She asked, "Who in the room speaks for you when you're not there?" Nobody, I realised. She offered to be that person. But she said, "You have to give me something to say." So I started asking for feedback every month, in writing. I volunteered for the project the director cared about. I told Rebecca plainly what I wanted: team lead within a year. Eleven months later I got it. So ask, Elizabeth. And find your Rebecca.

qa.q: How many times did promotion lists come out without Sangeeta's name?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What was young Sangeeta feeling in the ladies' room?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt hurt and invisible, crying after being passed over twice.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sangeeta's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Rebecca's question about who speaks for her led to monthly written feedback, a visible project and a plainly stated goal, which gave her sponsor something to say.

qa.q: How might Rebecca Joseph have seen the young Sangeeta?
qa.a: Rebecca likely saw a talented but invisible colleague and felt moved to sponsor her, recognising the pattern.

passage: Ganga had spent a year preparing for the senior designer role, and then her manager, Yusuf, announced he was leaving in two weeks. The promotion committee would meet in a month, without him. Her stomach dropped. He was the only one who had seen her best work up close. She could wait and hope, or move fast. That evening she sent him a short note: "Before you go, could you give me honest feedback on where I'm short of senior level? And would you be willing to write a note for the committee?" Yusuf replied the next morning with a meeting invite. He was frank: her designs were excellent, but she avoided difficult conversations with clients. He wrote a detailed note for the committee and introduced her to Leela, a director who had seen one of her projects. Ganga spent the next month leading two tough client calls on purpose, and sent Leela a short summary of each.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling when Yusuf announced he was leaving?

passage:
The promotion list went up on a Friday, and Vishal's name wasn't on it. He spent the weekend rehearsing complaints.

On Monday he did something else. He booked thirty minutes with Ankita, a senior analyst from another team who had once reviewed his dashboard and been blunt about it. At the café downstairs, he said, "I want the honest version. What would have made my manager say yes?"

Ankita stirred her coffee for a moment. "You do excellent work that nobody sees. You fix problems at midnight and never mention it in reviews. And in meetings you only speak when asked."

It stung. Vishal wrote it all down anyway.

"Would you look at my goals for the next six months?" he asked. "And if you think I'm ready by then, would you say so in the calibration meeting?"

Ankita laughed. "That's the first time a junior has asked me that directly. Send me the goals. We'll meet once a month." Vishal walked back upstairs lighter than he'd felt all weekend.

qa.a: The promotion list went up on a Friday.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel when Ankita told him his work was invisible?
qa.a: Vishal felt stung and a little hurt, but he wrote it down, showing he was determined to use it; later he felt lighter.

qa.q: What small steps could Vishal take from Ankita's feedback?
qa.a: He could share one problem he solved in each review, speak once in every meeting without being asked, and keep monthly meetings with Ankita.

qa.q: How might Ankita see Vishal after the conversation?
qa.a: Ankita seems amused and impressed by his directness, and is willing to invest time as a mentor and perhaps a sponsor.

Farida set her laptop down on Uday's desk. "Can I ask something awkward?"

"Go ahead."

"What would it take for me to become a team lead in the next cycle?"

Uday leaned back. "Honestly? Your client work is strong. But you've never run a project end to end."

"Then can I run the Nashik rollout?"

"It's messy. Two vendors, a tight timeline."

"That's why I want it. And could we meet every two weeks, so you can tell me what's going wrong before it goes wrong?"

Uday looked at her for a long moment. "You're serious."

"I am. And one more thing. The director doesn't know me. Would you introduce me when we present the plan?"

He laughed. "You've thought about this."

"All weekend," Farida admitted. "My palms are sweating right now."

"Fine. Nashik is yours. Fortnightly check-ins. And I'll bring you to the director meeting."

Farida picked up her laptop, and her hands were still not quite steady.

passage:
For my first two years at the firm, I thought good work would speak for itself. It didn't. I watched people with half my output get the interesting projects.

What changed was a lunch with Vikas, a partner I'd worked for exactly once. I asked him, rather clumsily, why I kept being passed over. He said, "Sonali, nobody in the room when projects are assigned knows what you want." That shocked me. I'd assumed everyone knew.

So I told him. I wanted to lead audit engagements for small manufacturers. He said he couldn't promise anything, but he'd mention my name when the next one came up.

Three months later, one did. He mentioned my name. I was nervous for most of that engagement and made two embarrassing mistakes, which he pointed out privately.

I'm leading my second one now. Looking back, the brave part wasn't the work. It was saying out loud, to someone with influence, what I actually wanted.

qa.q: What kind of work did Sonali say she wanted to lead?
qa.a: She wanted to lead audit engagements for small manufacturers.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel when Vikas said nobody knew what she wanted?
qa.a: Sonali felt shocked, because she had assumed everyone knew, and perhaps a little foolish for waiting.

qa.q: What could someone in Sonali's early position try, based on her story?
qa.a: Tell a senior person with influence exactly what role they want, ask them to mention their name, and accept private feedback on mistakes.

qa.q: How might Vikas see his role in Sonali's growth?
qa.a: Vikas probably sees himself as a sponsor who opened one door and gave honest feedback, while leaving the work itself to her.

Mentor's note. Sarika, team lead, product design.
Dolma, 24, asked me last month how to get promoted. I told her the truth: she does excellent work, but nobody outside our team knows it, and she never asks for feedback.
She took it seriously. She started asking after every project, "What's one thing I could have done better?" She wrote down the answers, even the harsh ones, and I saw her wince at a couple. She also asked if I'd introduce her to Arun from the strategy team, who sits on promotion panels. She presented her research at his team meeting.
At our last check-in, we wrote a growth plan together: skills to build, projects to lead, and a review date in six months.
She's still quiet in big meetings. But her name comes up now when leaders talk about who's ready.

Friday
Karthik writing. Two years at this company. Performance review today: "meets expectations". I was sure I'd get "exceeds". Came home and sulked through dinner.
Then I called Vishal Sir, my old manager, who moved to another division. He didn't sugarcoat it. "Do you know what your manager thinks 'exceeds' looks like?" I didn't. I'd never asked.
He told me three things:
Ask your manager for specific examples of what the next level does.
Ask for feedback every month, not once a year.
Find someone senior who knows your work and will speak for you when you're not in the room.
It stung that I'd been waiting to be noticed instead of asking. On Monday, I'm booking a thirty-minute chat with my manager, with those questions written down.

qa.a: Karthik felt disappointed and sulky, having expected "exceeds".

qa.a: Asking the manager for specific examples of the next level, because it makes the goal clear before anything else.

qa.q: How might Karthik's manager see the chat on Monday?
qa.a: The manager would probably appreciate the initiative and find it easier to guide someone who asks directly.
